title: Bram and the Lost Hedgehog
markdown:
In the rugged peaks of Misty Kettle, where clouds often brushed the mountain tops, lived Bram. A very large ogre, hands as big as dinner plates, voice that could rumble like faraway thunder. His heart was not thunderous. Soft and warm as a hearth on a chilly evening. He lived in a snug cottage among ancient pines: sweet pine needles, his mother’s famous berry scones, cheerful glow-moss on the hearth. Sturdy moss-covered stones. Windows onto rolling green hills and sky-blue lakes.

His most cherished companion was not another ogre, nor a grumpy troll, but a creature so tiny it could fit in the palm of his enormous hand. Bramble, his pet hedgehog. A marvel of prickles and snuffles, eyes like tiny dark beads sparkling with mischief. He loved to curl into a tight spiky ball when Bram scratched his little back just so. Rustle of delight, dry leaves skittering, at a juicy grub or a sweet sliver of dewdrop nectar. In the evenings Bram would hold him near the glow-moss until the prickles warmed, and Bramble would fall asleep as if the moss itself were a second cottage. Bram whispered secrets in a rumble made soft as a stream: cloud shapes, the funny way mountain goats wore their beards, the exact window where the lake turned sky-blue first.

One sunny afternoon, sky a vast bright blue, Bram tended his patch of glow-moss, humming a hearty ogre-tune. Bramble, ever curious, had been exploring near the edge of the Whispering Woods: ancient trees, silver moss, dappled sunlight. Secrets rustled on the breeze. Bram looked up, expecting a twitching nose under a fern. Only emerald fronds and a busy bumblebee.

“Bramble? Are you playing hide-and-seek again?”

A worried flutter from above. Whisper the Wren, feathers ruffled as if she’d flown through a sudden gust. “He went that way. Under a big mossy log, the one that looks like a sleeping giant’s elbow.”

Bram’s heart lurched like a hiccup. Darkening trees, fainter sunlight. A sigh like the softest gust. Grumbles the Goat, beard as wise as an old professor, hooves that knew every mountain path, nudged his leg. “Baa-rilliant it is to worry.” Which Bram understood to mean: tricky, but together.

He could not venture deeper without a plan. With Whisper flitting ahead like a tiny scout and Grumbles walking steadfastly beside him, comforting rhythm of hooves, he set off toward the tallest twistiest tower on the highest peak: home of Professor Fizzwick, spectacles sparkling with ancient wisdom, beard smelling faintly of toasted marshmallows and stardust.

The journey was long and winding. Steps heavy with concern. He clutched a smooth grey comfort-stone in his large pocket, coolness a small anchor. Pine gave way to thinner air. A stream crossed the path and Grumbles paused to drink, beard dripping, as if even a goat needed a moment that was not a search. Whisper circled once and came back. Bram imagined Bramble so small and alone, tiny legs tired, and he did not rush the stream. He waited until Grumbles was ready. That, too, was a kind of listening.

The wiggly tower leaned as if telling secrets to the clouds. Professor Fizzwick opened the door: kindly, ancient, robes embroidered with shimmering constellations, eyes twinkling behind thick round lenses. “Ah, Bram. And Grumbles. And little Whisper, perched so bravely. Has a cloud tumbled down, or has a star gone astray?”

Bram, a bit shy, explained. “My Bramble is lost. He’s very small, and the woods are so very big.” He held out an empty hand, imagining Bramble curled warm and safe.

Fizzwick stroked his singed beard, a wisp of smoke from its tip. “A small hedgehog and a vast wood. A classic conundrum. Like finding a single blueberry in a whole pie. What does Bramble like best? What makes his little heart sing?”

Bram thought hard. “The juiciest beetles, the ones that wriggle most. The sweetest dewdrop nectar, especially from moon-petaled flowers. And he loves to hide in warm soft things. He once fell asleep in a ball of yarn and I couldn’t find him for hours.”

Fizzwick’s eyes lit up. “Warm soft things. Dewdrop nectar.” He shuffled to a table of shimmering bottles, bubbling beakers, jars of herbs that smelled of sunshine. A tiny crystalline vial glowing with soft internal light. “Concentrated Sunshine-in-a-Bottle. Honey, warm meadows, happy dreams.” A basket of colourful feathers. “Whispering Winds Feathers. They carry the scent of the sweetest highland flowers. If we were to combine these…”

A gentle swirl of wand, a puff of shimmering sweet-smelling dust, an incantation like the hum of a contented bumblebee. A small glowing orb, pulsing golden, scent of warm blankets and summer flowers. “Place this near where you last saw him. Its warmth will draw him. Its scent will guide him like a magical breadcrumb trail. Sometimes the smallest creatures are found not by shouting or rushing, but by quiet listening.”

Renewed hope, like Whisper’s wings. Bram carried the orb, surprisingly warm, smelling like a perfect summer meadow. Back at the woods’ edge he placed it on a bed of soft emerald moss, right where Whisper had seen Bramble disappear.

Then he sat quietly, large frame making a surprisingly small circle on the forest floor, and listened. Rustling leaves, the forest sighing. Chirping birds. The gentle hum of the woods. A beetle, the wriggly sort Bramble favoured, crossed a sun-patch and went on about its business. Grumbles chewed his cud, a comforting weight. Whisper scanned every nook from a branch overhead. Bram did not call. He did not part the first thicket he saw. He let the orb do the inviting, and he let the woods be woods.

After a few moments: a tiny familiar rustling from a thicket of brambles not far from the orb. Then a faint happy snuffle. Bram’s heart did a little dance.

He got up slowly, carefully. Parted thorny branches, large hands surprisingly delicate. There, nestled among soft fallen leaves, sniffing the glowing orb with great interest: Bramble. Little nose twitching. Seeing Bram, he uncurled and waddled with surprising speed toward his giant friend.

“Bramble.” A joyous rumble, relief like a happy thunderclap. He scooped his tiny pet into his massive hand. Bramble snuggled in, prickles soft against warm skin. The orb’s glow faded slightly as Bramble nudged it, as if thanking it.

They walked home, sun casting long friendly shadows. The berry-scone smell met them before the cottage door. Bram whispered, “Better when we’re together.” Bramble snuffled, safe in big gentle hands, and promptly fell asleep as if the woods had been only another warm hiding place. The highlands did not need a speech about friendship. They had a hedgehog, a wren, a goat, and an orb going quietly dim.
characters: Bram (young ogre with a soft heart), Bramble (a hedgehog who loves warm hiding places)
